scenes.title: Your score
sentences: If your score is 5 or higher, you are at high risk of developing prediabetes.
That means your blood sugar may already be creeping up.
Let's see what that means.

scenes.title: How common it is
sentences: Prediabetes is very common.
About 98 million adults in the United States have it. That's more than one in three.
And most of them don't know.
The risk score runs from zero to ten. Five or higher is the high-risk zone.

scenes.title: What happens inside
sentences: Here's what's going on inside your body.
Insulin works like a key. It opens the doors of your cells, so sugar from your food can get in and give you energy.
With insulin resistance, the locks get stuck, and your cells stop listening.
Your body makes even more insulin, to push harder.
Over time it can't keep up, and sugar builds up in your blood. That is prediabetes.

scenes.title: What raises your score
sentences: Your score adds up things that make diabetes more likely.
Getting older. Having a parent, brother or sister with diabetes. Carrying extra weight. Not being very active.
High blood pressure. Diabetes during a past pregnancy. Unhealthy cholesterol. Or a condition called P C O S.
The more of these that apply to you, the higher your score.

scenes.title: The blood tests
sentences: Only a blood test can tell you for sure. Doctors check three numbers.
First, fasting sugar, after eight hours without food. Under 100 is normal. 100 to 125 is prediabetes. 126 or more is diabetes.
Second, A1C, your average sugar over three months. Under 5.7 percent is normal. 5.7 to 6.4 is prediabetes. 6.5 or more is diabetes.
Third, a sugary drink test, checked two hours later. Under 140 is normal. 140 to 199 is prediabetes. 200 or more is diabetes.

scenes.title: The good news
sentences: Now, the good news. Prediabetes can often be reversed.
In a big study, lifestyle changes cut the chance of getting type 2 diabetes by fifty-eight percent.
People lost about seven percent of their weight.
And walked briskly for about 150 minutes a week. That's half an hour, five days a week.
Eat more vegetables and whole grains, and drink fewer sugary drinks.
If your score is 5 or higher, ask your doctor for a blood test.
This video is for learning, not diagnosis. Sources are listed on screen and on the page.
